claim: The Russian Second Army under Samsonov advanced into East Prussia on 20-21 August 1914 (New Style), i.e. 7-8 August Old Style; Zhilinsky, commanding both armies, was anxious to press the German Eighth Army after Gumbinnen.
Division and corps commanders complained of poor supply and the pace demanded by Zhilinsky; the two armies were too far apart to help each other; the Germans read intercepted radio messages.
The battle was fought 26-30 August 1914 (New Style), the 13th to 17th Old Style; the Second Army was almost completely destroyed and Samsonov killed himself.
The First Army was turned back about a fortnight later (Masurian Lakes, 9-14 September New Style).
note: Confirm.

claim: Zhilinsky's position is characterized as: the enemy is going back and has to be kept going.
note: Characterization of a documented attitude, not a quotation.

claim: Przemyśl surrendered on 22 March 1915 (New Style), 9 March Old Style; the garrison of about 117,000 surrendered with nine generals.

Austro-Hungarian casualties January to April 1915 in the Carpathians were officially reported as 800,000, mostly from weather and disease; Russian casualties were nearly as high but easier to replace.
note: The source is a Wikipedia summary of the Austro-Hungarian figure; the Russian comparison needs a better source.

claim: The Russian armies were short of shells and rifles in the spring of 1915.
note: Widely stated; see also the existing retreat node (Brusilov's report).

claim: The German attack at Gorlice in May turned the Carpathian positions.
note: 2 May New Style; the existing retreat node is dated 19 April Old Style.

claim: The South-Western Front attacked on 4 June 1916 (New Style), 22 May Old Style; Brusilov's request for supporting offensives was denied and Evert's Western Front did not attack until 18 June.
Evert's attack from 2 July took about five kilometres at a cost of about 80,000 men.
On 17 June Alekseyev transferred the Third Army to Brusilov; Bezobrazov's Guards Army was added, bringing the front to about 700,000 men against 421,000.
Artillery preparation for Kovel began on 24 July (New Style), the main assaults ran from 28 July, the advance was halted by 8 August and Brusilov suspended the operation on 9 August.
note: Converted to Old Style in the text: 11, 15, 26 and 27 July.

claim: Gurko's Special Army took part in the Stokhod fighting.
note: Check the order of battle.

claim: Brusilov wanted to go on for Kovel.
note: Characterization of a documented aim.

claim: Romania entered the war on 27 August 1916 (New Style), 14 August Old Style, after the success of the Brusilov offensive.
The Russians moved three divisions to help the Romanians, and they were not properly equipped.
Bucharest fell on 6 December 1916 (New Style), 23 November Old Style; Russia then had to send large reinforcements to the Romanian front to prevent a German advance into the south of Russia.
Alekseyev's position is characterized as: the Romanian front must not be allowed to take the armies from the main one.
note: From the research pass; not recorded. Alekseyev is reported to have regarded Romania's entry as a burden. Verify or remove.

claim: Kerensky sent telegraphic orders instituting the death penalty at the front on 12 July 1917 (Old Style), in response to an ultimatum from Kornilov.
note: From a web-search summary of this page; confirm on the page or in a source for the ultimatum.

claim: The Provisional Government abolished the death penalty in the army in March 1917.
note: Confirm the date.

claim: Kornilov was appointed commander of the South-Western Front in July and Supreme Commander in place of Brusilov on 18 July Old Style (31 July New Style).

Kerensky sent Kornilov a dismissal telegram on 27 August 1917 (Old Style); the march on Petrograd ran 28-31 August (10-13 September New Style) and collapsed through low morale and desertion; the affair ended bloodlessly on 30 August.
The Petrograd Soviet created the Committee for the Struggle Against Counter-Revolution on 28 August.
Kornilov ordered General Krymov's Third Cavalry Corps toward Petrograd following the German occupation of Riga.
Kornilov was arrested and Alekseyev returned as Chief of Staff at the end of August.
note: The Alekseyev dossier says he returned briefly as Chief of Staff; check the date of the arrest (1 September).

claim: Whether Kornilov meant to take power or to carry out an arrangement agreed with the government is disputed; an intermediary (Lvov) carried messages the two men understood differently.
note: Dispute carried in the choice's dispute field. Cite a source for the Lvov exchange.

claim: On 9 November 1917 (Old Style) the Council of People's Commissars ordered Dukhonin to begin armistice negotiations; he refused, saying such an order could come only from a government sustained by the army and the country, and was dismissed; Krylenko was named in his place.
note: The page gives 22 November (New Style).

claim: On 20 November (3 December New Style) Dukhonin surrendered to Krylenko at Mogilev and was killed by a mob at the railway station despite Krylenko's attempt to prevent it.
note: Accounts vary on who ordered it.
